subject: geography
title: Networks: Transport, ICT and Finance
welcome_lead: Containers, fibre-optic cables and SWIFT messages — the infrastructure of globalisation.
meta_desc: IBDP Geography HL Adventure: transport, ICT and financial networks in the global system.
final_note: You have traced the wires and routes of globalisation. Networks confer power and produce vulnerabilities.

concepts.def: Standardisation of shipping containers (TEU) from the 1950s, transforming global logistics.
Fibre-optic cables crossing oceans, carrying over 95% of intercontinental data traffic.
Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, messaging network central to global payments.
Network model with central hubs connecting peripheral nodes, common in aviation.
Strategic geographic constraint on movement, e.g. Strait of Hormuz, Suez Canal.
Chinese strategy launched 2013 financing infrastructure across Eurasia, Africa and Latin America.

walkthroughs.body_html: Containerisation (Malcolm McLean, 1956) cut handling costs dramatically. Megaports (Shanghai, Singapore, Rotterdam) and hubs handle hundreds of millions of TEUs annually. Choke points like Suez (Ever Given incident 2021), Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb illustrate vulnerabilities in maritime networks.

Roughly 500 submarine cables, totalling over 1.4 million km, carry the world's internet traffic. Companies like Google, Meta and Microsoft increasingly own or lease cables. Concentrated landing sites and a few cable-laying ships create resilience concerns.

SWIFT messages support about 42 million transactions a day across more than 200 countries. Sanctions (e.g. exclusions of Iranian and some Russian banks) demonstrate how financial networks become instruments of power. Alternatives like CIPS (China) and SPFS (Russia) are emerging.
